meta.title: Who really said "I do not feel obliged to believe that the same God who has endowed us with senses, reason, and intellect has intended us to forgo their use"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Galileo, from his 1615 Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina. The Italian is public domain; the English wording people quote is not.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I do not feel obliged to believe that the same God who has endowed us with senses, reason, and intellect has intended us to forgo their use'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Galileo — the 1615 Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina. We read the Italian original; the familiar English is a modern translation.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Galileo wrote it in his Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615) ↗, arguing that scripture was never meant to settle questions the senses and reason can settle. We read the Italian original in Favaro’s Edizione Nazionale, vol. 5, p. 317 ↗. The sentence people quote is the first half of a longer one.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina
Le opere di Galileo Galilei, Edizione Nazionale, ed. Antonio Favaro, vol. 5 (1895), p. 317
A twentieth-century translation; the standard modern English version of the letter is Stillman Drake’s (1957)

source.excerpt: Ma che quell’istesso Dio che ci ha dotati di sensi, di discorso e d’intelletto, abbia voluto, posponendo l’uso di questi, darci con altro mezo le notizie che per quelli possiamo conseguire, sì che anco in quelle conclusioni naturali, che o dalle sensate esperienze o dalle necessarie dimostrazioni ci vengono esposte innanzi a gli occhi e all’intelletto, doviamo negare il senso e la ragione, non credo che sia necessario il crederlo.
trail: The English wording sits in the sourced section of Wikiquote’s Galileo page ↗, under the Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615), where it appears in full rather than in the truncated popular form.

We located the Italian original directly, on Italian Wikisource’s transcription of Favaro’s Edizione Nazionale, vol. 5, p. 317 ↗ — the same critical edition whose next pages carry Galileo’s marginal note on Cardinal Baronio.
No pre-1931 English rendering of this wording could be found: searches of Project Gutenberg and English Wikisource returned nothing, which is why the English is treated as in-copyright.
source.cutTag: Italian original, Favaro ed., vol. 5, p. 317
source.excerptNote: The Italian ends on “non credo che sia necessario il crederlo” — literally “I do not think it necessary to believe it”. The familiar English “I do not feel obliged to believe” moves that clause to the front, and the popular quotation then stops halfway, dropping “and by some other means to give us knowledge which we can attain by them”.

source.rightsNote: Two rights questions sit on this page. Galileo’s 1615 Italian, as printed in Favaro’s 1895 Edizione Nazionale ↗, is long in the public domain. The English wording people actually quote is a twentieth-century translation and is not. We classify by the translation shown, and we could not confirm by direct reading which published translation this exact string is — the standard modern English version, Stillman Drake’s Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo (1957), is lending-restricted — so no translator is named as the rights holder.

author.name: Galileo Galilei
author.heading: About Galileo Galilei
author.bio: Galileo Galilei turned the newly invented telescope on the night sky and found moons around Jupiter, mountains on the Moon and phases on Venus — observations that made the Copernican system hard to dismiss. He argued, in Italian and in public, that the book of nature was written in mathematics and open to anyone who would look. In 1633 the Roman Inquisition convicted him of suspicion of heresy, and he spent his last years under house arrest.

copyAttribution: "I do not feel obliged to believe that the same God who has endowed us with senses, reason, and intellect has intended us to forgo their use and by some other means to give us knowledge which we can attain by them." — Galileo Galilei, Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina, 1615. Italian original in Le opere di Galileo Galilei, Edizione Nazionale, ed. Antonio Favaro, vol. 5 (1895), p. 317. The popular quotation stops halfway; the English is a modern translation, not Galileo’s words.

misattribution.heading: What people get wrong
misattribution.intro: The attribution is sound — this really is Galileo. Two smaller things travel with it that are not.

items.why: The quotation almost always stops at “forgo their use”. Galileo’s sentence continues “and by some other means to give us knowledge which we can attain by them” — the clause that makes the argument an argument rather than a slogan.
Galileo wrote in Italian. The English sentence is a modern translator’s, and the Italian it renders is structured the other way round, ending rather than beginning on the refusal to believe.

misattribution.truthLine: Correctly attributed, commonly truncated, and always read in somebody else’s English — the Italian is here ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In 1615 Galileo was not yet on trial, but the Copernican argument was already being fought on scriptural ground. The Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina is his attempt to settle the jurisdictional question before it reached him: what the Bible is for, and what it is not for.

His answer is the sentence above. If God gave us senses and reason, it would be strange of Him to expect us to reach by revelation the things those faculties can reach on their own. Eighteen years later the Inquisition decided otherwise.
detailsBody: The same letter carries Galileo’s report of a churchman’s quip that the intention of the Holy Ghost is to teach us how one goes to heaven, not how heaven goes — a line he attributes in the margin to Cardinal Baronio, three pages later in the same critical edition.
context.pull: If God gave us the instruments, He can hardly have meant us to leave them in the drawer.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote’s sourced section files the full sentence under the Letter to the Grand Duchess Christina (1615).
The Italian original stands at Favaro’s Edizione Nazionale vol. 5, p. 317: “Ma che quell’istesso Dio che ci ha dotati di sensi, di discorso e d’intelletto… non credo che sia necessario il crederlo.”
Drake’s Discoveries and Opinions of Galileo (1957) is listed as the edition carrying the full text of the letter in English.
